name: Puente Romano, Mérida (fall of Mérida)
story: Mérida was the key road and rail junction between the Nationalist south and north. Around 2,600 militiamen and loyal forces held the Guadiana line against columns under Asensio, Castejón and Tella. On 10 August the Legion's 5th Bandera rushed the 2,000-year-old Roman bridge, which the defenders had mined; the charges were not fired (Nationalist accounts credit Cmdr. Luis Alarcón de la Lastra with disarming them) and the troops broke into the city. Mérida's capture linked Seville with Mola's northern zone. Mass detentions followed: the bullring, the Santo Domingo convent and the barracks became prison camps, and executions took place at the cemetery wall.
see: The Roman bridge (now pedestrian) over the Guadiana, where the assault crossed; in the town, the town hall on Plaza de España and a memorial at the municipal cemetery to the victims of the repression.
plan: Free, always open; walk the bridge from the Alcazaba end (10 min). The cemetery memorial is a short drive north of the centre.

boxes.text: Casualties of the fighting are not reliably known; numbers for the subsequent repression in Mérida vary between studies.
